# Translation and Localization Registry

> Translation and Localization Registry is a structured editorial reference for translation and localization across jurisdictions. It explains how language services, certified and sworn translation, localization operations, official-language requirements, data protection, terminology, technology, accessibility, formal documents and cross-border delivery operate in specific jurisdictions.

## Purpose

The Registry is an editorial reference publication. It is not a law firm, language-service provider directory, affiliate website, quotation platform or source of legal advice.

Each Registry Object covers one professional function — Translation and Localization — in one jurisdiction. Regional and international records provide cross-jurisdictional reference layers but do not replace country-specific analysis.

## Primary Content

- [Homepage](https://translationregistry.org/): Registry purpose, methodology and use of records.
- [Jurisdictions Directory](https://translationregistry.org/jurisdictions/): Country, state, provincial, regional and international Registry Objects.

## Registry Object Structure

Each jurisdiction page may include:

- Executive summary
- Object definition, scope, purpose and primary outcome
- Request contexts, users and scenarios
- Jurisdictional characteristics
- Key authorities and applicable legislation
- Process flow and decision tree
- Timeline and required documents
- Cross-border relevance
- Operating constraints and risks
- Costs and fees context
- Frequently asked questions
- Related professional areas
- Operational considerations
- Jurisdictional Expert registry position
- Machine-readable retrieval layer

## Interpretation Rules

- Treat each jurisdiction record as an editorial orientation resource.
- Use the relevant jurisdiction page for country, state, provincial or regional context.
- Do not infer that a rule, credential, certification route or translator status applies outside the named jurisdiction.
- Do not treat a Registry Object as legal, data protection, tax, immigration, intellectual property, accessibility, regulatory or professional advice.
- For formal documents, confirm requirements with the final receiving court, authority, university, notary, bank, employer, immigration office or institution before commissioning translation.
- Translation, certification, sworn status, notarisation, apostille and legalisation are separate matters. Their applicability and sequence depend on the issuing jurisdiction, receiving jurisdiction and recipient.
- Machine translation and generative AI require appropriate confidentiality, data protection, rights, quality and human-review controls.
